t0: Alder Street runs four blocks from the market to the canal bridge, lined with brick shopfronts, a baker, a shoe repair and a chemist under faded awnings. Delivery vans double-park at noon, and the plane trees along the kerb are still half grown.

At the start, Alder Street is a narrow commercial run of two- and three-storey brick, its ground floors let to a baker, a cobbler and a chemist. Traffic is steady, the awnings are sun-bleached, and young plane trees stand in the kerbstones.

Alder Street, four blocks of brick between the market and the canal bridge, carries the ordinary trade of the quarter: bread, shoes, medicines, a pub on the corner. Vans block the lane at midday and the kerbside plane trees are still slender.
1day: Alder Street looks exactly as it did. The baker has sold out by ten, a van has scraped the chemist's downpipe, and someone has chalked the day's prices on the pub board. Nothing has changed that a photograph would show.

One turn of the sun and Alder Street is unchanged: the same shutters go up, the same vans double-park, the same four blocks of brick. Only the litter in the gutter is new, and a delivery crate left outside the cobbler's door.

The street is indistinguishable from yesterday. Bread, shoes and medicines are sold in the same doorways, the awnings are one day more faded, and a fresh scuff marks the kerb where a lorry mounted it in the morning.
1week: A week on, Alder Street is the same street with small news. The cobbler has been shut three days with a bad back, scaffolding has gone up over the chemist, and the pub has a new sign. The trade, the traffic and the buildings are unchanged.

Seven days have made no structural difference. Scaffolding now stands against one shopfront, one business has been dark since Tuesday, and the market's weekly rhythm has come round once. The brick, the awnings and the plane trees are exactly as before.

Alder Street after a week: same buildings, same tenants, one shutter down for illness and one facade under scaffolding for repointing. The week's rubbish has been collected twice. Nothing that would appear on a map has altered at all.
6months: Half a year has turned the street's weather over. The plane trees are bare, the awnings are rolled in, and braziers stand outside the pub. The chemist has been repainted and the cobbler's lease has passed to a phone repair shop; everything else holds.

Six months later the season is inverted: cold light, bare branches, salt on the pavement. One shopfront has changed hands and another has been repainted, but the four blocks of brick, the kerb line and the trade of the street are what they were.

The street has crossed into the opposite season. Where there were leaves and shade there is now bare timber and early dark. Of the shops, one has closed and reopened under a new name; the rest keep their doorways and their hours.
1year: A full year round, and Alder Street has come back to its own season: leaves out, awnings down, vans in the lane at noon. Two of the twelve shopfronts have changed hands in the interval, and the chemist has extended into the unit beside it.

The year closes where it began, the same light on the same brick. Turnover has been modest: a phone repair shop where the cobbler was, a cafe where the stationer was, and new paint on three facades. The street's shape is untouched.

One year on the street is recognisably itself, with the season come round again. Perhaps a sixth of the tenancies are new, the plane trees are a little taller, and a pothole at the bridge end has been patched twice.
10years: Ten years have turned nearly every tenancy over. The baker and the chemist are gone; there are two cafes, a nail bar, a betting shop and three empty units. The corner pub has been converted into flats and the plane trees now shade the whole kerb.

After a decade the buildings stand but the street is not the same business. Most signs are new, rents have doubled, one block has been demolished and rebuilt in glass, and the market end has been pedestrianised. Only the alignment and the brick are continuous.

A decade of turnover: the shoe repair, the stationer and the pub have all closed, a supermarket has taken three units at once, and the canal end has been redeveloped. The trees are mature, the kerbs re-laid, the street name unchanged.
100years: A century later almost nothing of the original street survives. The brick terraces were cleared for a road widening and replaced by concrete blocks; the canal bridge has been rebuilt twice. The name Alder Street persists on a plate, attached to a slightly different line.

After a hundred years the street exists chiefly as a name and a right of way. Its buildings were bombed, cleared, rebuilt and rebuilt again; the market is a car park; the plane trees were felled and replanted. The trade bears no relation to the old.

A century has replaced the fabric entirely. The four blocks are now two long blocks of offices and flats, the canal is culverted, and the one surviving fragment of Victorian brick is a listed facade pinned to a newer frame.
1000years: A thousand years on, the street survives only as an alignment. A lane still runs from the old market ground to the crossing, because the ground makes people walk that way, but nothing standing on it is older than a few generations, and the name is lost.

After a millennium, Alder Street is a line in the subsoil. Later streets have inherited part of its course by habit; the rest is under a rail embankment. Its buildings are a metre of brick rubble and ash beneath the present pavement.

Ten centuries have erased the street as a street. Archaeology could recover the cellar walls and the kerbstones; walking the quarter, one would notice only that a modern path runs, for no visible reason, along the old line to the water.
10000years: Ten thousand years later there is no street and no city on the site. A low rise of brick-flecked soil marks where the quarter stood, cut by a stream that has shifted its bed. Woodland and scrub cover the ground and the alignment is gone.

After a hundred centuries the place has reverted to landscape. What was Alder Street is a band of dark, artefact-rich earth two metres down, overlain by alluvium. Nothing on the surface preserves a line, a name or a direction.

Ten millennia have taken the street down to a stratum. The river has meandered across the site twice, sorting the rubble; trees stand where the market was. Only a buried horizon of burnt clay and glass records that anyone built here.
1000000years: A million years later the site is geology. Tectonic uplift and repeated glaciation have stripped or buried the whole valley; the old ground surface is either eroded away or sealed under tens of metres of till. No trace of a street is recoverable.

After a million years the question of the street has no answer at the scale of streets. The coastline has moved tens of kilometres, ice sheets have crossed the region and retreated, and the rock beneath has been planed. The city is a smear, not a layer.

A million years has dissolved every human scale. If anything survives it is a thin, discontinuous lens of unusual minerals within river gravels, indistinguishable in the field. The valley itself has been recut and the sea has come and gone twice.

t0: Mount Caldreth stands 2,400 metres above the valley, a granite mass with a snow cap that lasts into July, three cirques cut into its north face, and a talus apron at its foot. A footpath switchbacks to the shoulder and stops there.

At the outset the mountain is a weathered granite pyramid, 2,400 metres high, ribbed with snow gullies and skirted by scree. Krummholz gives out at two thousand metres; above that there is bare rock, ice and lichen.

Caldreth rises 2,400 metres in grey granite, its north face held in three cirques, its summit ridge broken into blocks by frost. Meltwater streams leave the talus on the south side and gather in a small tarn.
1day: After a day the mountain is identical. A few cubic metres of snow have slid from a gully, one block has come off the ridge and lodged in the talus, and the tarn is a centimetre higher. No measurement at human scale would show a change.

One day on, nothing has happened to the mountain that anyone could see. Clouds have crossed it, the snowline has moved a few metres with the sun, and a little rock has fallen. Its height, its faces and its outline are exactly as before.

A single day leaves Caldreth untouched. The weather has changed, the shadows have gone round once, and frost has worked a few millimetres further into a crack. The granite, the cirques and the summit ridge are unaltered.
1week: A week has changed only the weather on the mountain. Half a metre of new snow lies above two thousand metres and has already begun to settle, and a small slab avalanche has run in the north cirque. The rock itself is unchanged.

Seven days later the mountain is the same mountain. Snow has fallen and partly melted, the tarn has risen and fallen, and a walker has rebuilt the cairn on the shoulder. Nothing structural has moved at all.

After a week the only differences are surface ones: new snow in the gullies, a swollen meltwater stream, fresh rockfall dust on the talus. Caldreth's height and shape are identical to within a millimetre. The cirques hold the same ice they held seven days ago.
6months: Six months have turned the season over on the mountain. The snow cap now reaches down to the treeline, the tarn is frozen, and the footpath is impassable. The rock beneath is unchanged; only its covering has inverted.

Half a year later Caldreth is in its other condition: white to the shoulder, the cirques loaded, the streams silent under ice. Freeze and thaw have prised a little more scree onto the apron. The form of the mountain is the same.

After six months the mountain wears winter instead of summer. Snow depth on the north face has trebled and the summer path is gone. Measured as rock, Caldreth has lost a few tonnes to frost shatter out of many billions.
1year: A year round, the mountain is back where it started: snow cap into July, tarn open, path clear to the shoulder. Perhaps a few hundred tonnes of rock have moved from face to talus, which is nothing against its bulk. Its height is unchanged.

One year later Caldreth is indistinguishable from its first description. The season has completed a circuit and returned. Erosion has lowered the summit by a fraction of a millimetre and widened one crack; no survey at this scale could detect it.

The year has closed with the mountain exactly as it began. The same gullies hold the same late snow and the same streams leave the talus. Only the tally of fallen blocks at the foot has grown very slightly.
10years: Ten years have made no visible difference to the mountain. The glacierette in the north cirque has retreated some tens of metres, a rockfall has scarred one buttress, and the treeline has crept a little upslope. The summit is the same height.

After a decade Caldreth is unchanged in form. Its ice is smaller, its talus slightly deeper, and a marked path has been eroded into a gully by boots. Photographs taken ten years apart would need annotation to tell them apart.

A decade of weather has removed a few millimetres from the summit and a few thousand tonnes from the faces. The mountain is the same mountain: the same cirques, the same ridge, the same profile against the sky.
100years: A century later the mountain still stands 2,400 metres high, to within a centimetre or two. The small glacier is gone, leaving bare rock and a new pond, and one buttress has collapsed into a fresh scree cone. The outline is recognisable from old photographs.

After a hundred years Caldreth would be identified without hesitation from its first description. Erosion has taken about a centimetre off the summit. What has changed is the ice, which has left the north cirque, and the treeline, which has risen a hundred metres.

A century has altered the mountain's furniture and not the mountain. The permanent snow is now intermittent, one gully has been scoured out by a debris flow, and the tarn has silted. Height, mass and shape are effectively identical.
1000years: A thousand years on, Caldreth has lost perhaps a metre of summit and gained a broader talus apron. A glacial advance and retreat has polished the upper cirques. Anyone who knew the mountain would still know it; the profile has barely moved.

After a millennium the mountain is the same landform with slightly rounded edges. One large rock avalanche has removed a shoulder and left a scar visible from the valley. Its height is within a metre or two of the original figure.

Ten centuries of frost and water have lowered Caldreth by about a metre and deepened its gullies. Ice has occupied and abandoned the north face at least once. The summit ridge is still broken granite at 2,400 metres.
10000years: Ten thousand years have begun to show. Repeated glaciation has widened the cirques into a sharper horn, the talus has advanced across the valley floor, and the summit is several metres lower. The mountain is still plainly a mountain, but the details have been recut.

After a hundred centuries Caldreth has been visibly reworked. Glaciers have come and gone, backwearing the north face and leaving moraines below it, and the tarn has been replaced by a larger lake. Height is down perhaps five to ten metres.

Ten millennia have carved rather than destroyed. The cirques are deeper, the aretes thinner, the valley below over-deepened by ice. The summit stands a few metres lower than it did and the scree apron is twice its old extent.
1000000years: A million years later Caldreth is a different landform. Denudation at a tenth of a millimetre a year has removed on the order of a hundred metres, if uplift has not matched it; the peak is a rounded mass and the cirques have merged into one broad bowl.

After a million years the mountain has been largely unbuilt. Its granite core is exposed at a lower level, the sharp ridge has been reduced to a broad shoulder, and drainage has captured the old valley. Nothing of its outline survives recognisably.

A million years of erosion and uplift have left something at this location that may still be high ground, but it is not the described mountain. Hundreds of metres of rock have gone to the sea as sand; the faces, gullies and tarn are erased.

t0: The orchard covers six hectares: three hundred apple trees in twenty rows, fifteen years old, in full blossom. Bees are working the rows, the grass between them is newly cut, and the irrigation lines have just been charged for the season.

At first the orchard stands in white blossom, three hundred grafted apples on semi-dwarf stock spaced six metres apart. The ground is green and mown, the frames of the hail nets are up, and a hive sits at the end of every fourth row.

Six hectares of apple trees, fifteen years old and at their productive peak, are in flower. Petals cover the alleys, the pruning wounds from winter have callused over, and the grower is watching the forecast for a late frost.
1day: A day later the orchard is the same orchard in the same week of its year. A little more blossom has opened, a little has fallen, and the bees have worked another eight hours. Nothing about the trees or the rows has changed.

One day on, the blossom is perhaps a day further along: more petals on the ground, the earliest flowers already setting. The grass is a few millimetres taller. Otherwise the six hectares are exactly as described.

After a single day the orchard shows only the ordinary progress of flowering. Pollination has continued, one row has been sprayed, and a cold night has damaged a few blossoms on the low ground. The structure is untouched.
1week: A week has carried the orchard out of full bloom. Most petals are down, the alleys are white with them, and small green fruitlets are visible at the centres of the spent flowers. The trees and rows are otherwise unchanged.

Seven days later the blossom is over and fruit set has begun. The hives have been moved to the next block, the grass has been cut again, and the first thinning is being planned. The layout of the orchard is identical.

After a week the orchard has moved one step along its season: petal fall complete, fruitlets forming, leaves now the dominant colour. Three hundred trees in twenty rows over six hectares, exactly as before. The irrigation has run twice and the hail nets remain furled.
6months: Six months later the orchard is in the opposite part of its year. The fruit has been picked, the leaves are yellow and falling, the grass has been left long, and the hail nets are furled. The rows stand bare and wet.

Half a year on, the orchard is post-harvest and shutting down. Bins are stacked at the headland, windfalls rot in the alleys, and the trees are dropping their leaves. Nothing is in flower and nothing is growing.

After six months the orchard has inverted: blossom replaced by bare branches, mown green by leaf litter and mud. The crop is in store, pruning has not yet begun, and the irrigation has been drained for the winter.
1year: A year later the orchard is in blossom again. The trees are sixteen years old rather than fifteen, two have been replaced after canker, and the rest are marginally larger. Bees are working the rows and the alleys are mown as before.

One full year round, the orchard has returned to the state it began in: white bloom, warm days, hives at the row ends. A winter's pruning has opened the canopies slightly and last season's crop is long sold. It is recognisably the same picture.

The orchard has completed a circuit. It stands in flower for the sixteenth time, on the same six hectares in the same twenty rows, with three replacement whips where old trees failed. Only the rings in the wood record that a year has passed.
10years: Ten years on the orchard is past its best. The trees are twenty-five years old, tall and biennial in their bearing, and yields are down by a third. Four rows have been grubbed out and replanted with a newer variety on dwarfing stock.

After a decade the planting has aged. Canker and woolly aphid have taken a dozen trees, the canopies have closed over the alleys, and the grower has begun a phased replacement. The blossom still comes each spring, thinner than before.

A decade has turned a mature orchard into an old one. Trunks are thick and mossy, the hail net frames have rusted, and one block has already been replaced. The six hectares are still an orchard, still cropping, but not the same trees.
100years: A century later there is no orchard. The planting was grubbed out in its fourth decade, the ground was cropped in arable for a generation and then abandoned; the field is now rough scrub with a few feral apples along the old boundary.

After a hundred years the six hectares have passed through two other uses and come back to nothing in particular. Hawthorn and ash have colonised it; a line of gnarled apple trees on the hedge bank is the only sign that fruit was ever grown here.

A century has dissolved the orchard. Successor plantings failed, the holding was broken up, and the land is now half woodland and half a horse paddock. Seedling apples, descended from the original rootstocks, grow wild among the thorn.
1000years: A thousand years later the site is woodland with no memory of cultivation. Oak and ash have closed over it, and the plough marks and irrigation trenches survive only as faint soil features. Apple pollen persists in the sediment of the old pond.

After a millennium nothing above ground records an orchard. The six hectares are mature forest on a slope that has lost a little topsoil. Buried lines of compacted subsoil, where the rows once stood, are the last physical trace.

Ten centuries have made the place indistinguishable from the wood around it. The varieties that were planted are gone; wild crab apple is present, but no more than elsewhere. Only pollen cores and a soil horizon distinguish the ground.
10000years: Ten thousand years later the site's climate and vegetation belong to a different regime. The soil that held the orchard has been eroded and redeposited downslope. Nothing biological, chemical or structural marks the ground as having been planted.

After a hundred centuries the question of the orchard is unanswerable. The valley has been wooded and cleared several times, a stream has cut across the field, and the plough horizon has been truncated. No trace remains of the planting.

Ten millennia have removed even the traces. The pond has silted and its pollen record has been reworked, and the slope has lost half a metre of soil. What grows there now is whatever the present climate allows.
1000000years: A million years later the location is a geological one, not an agricultural one. The land surface has been stripped and rebuilt many times, and the cultivated apple as the orchard knew it no longer exists. Nothing of the orchard is recoverable in principle.

After a million years there is no site to speak of. Sea level has risen and fallen repeatedly, the drainage has been reorganised, and the soil of that field is sandstone somewhere else. The orchard is not merely gone but unlocatable.

A million years has outlasted the cultivar and probably the species. The ground has been under ice, under forest and under water; the described six hectares exist only as scattered grains within younger sediments. No sediment anywhere records that fruit was cultivated on that slope.

t0: The mayfly has just emerged onto the surface of the river and dried its wings. It is an adult of a few hours, with no working mouthparts and perhaps a day of life, and it is climbing the air above the riffle in the evening swarm.

At first the mayfly is newly winged, pale and soft, resting on a willow leaf above the water. Its gut is non-functional and its only remaining business is to moult once more and mate; its lifespan as an adult is about twenty-four hours.

A mayfly stands on the bankside vegetation an hour after leaving the water, wings held upright, body still soft. It will shed its final skin tonight and join the swarm. It cannot eat, and it will not live to see two sunsets.
1day: One day later the mayfly is dead. It mated in the evening swarm, the female dropped her eggs onto the riffle, and both spent adults fell onto the water within hours. The body is drifting downstream in the surface film.

After a day the animal's entire adult life is over. It moulted, flew, mated and fell; what remains is a spent husk on the water surface, being taken by trout and wagtails. Its eggs are on the gravel of the riffle.

Twenty-four hours has used the mayfly up completely. The swarm rose, paired and collapsed overnight, and the individual is now a dead insect in the drift with its wings flat on the water. Nothing of it is alive except its eggs.
1week: A week later there is no mayfly at all. The body was eaten or broke up in the current within a day or two of death. On the riverbed its eggs have not yet hatched; the individual is simply absent from the reach.

Seven days on, the animal has ceased to exist as a body. Its remains entered the food chain within hours. The river still has its evening swarms, made of other insects that emerged after it; this one is gone entirely.

After a week nothing physical of the mayfly persists. Scavengers and flow have dispersed it. What continues is the population: eggs on the gravel, nymphs of earlier cohorts in the silt, and a swarm every warm evening.
6months: Six months later the mayfly is long gone and its offspring are half-grown nymphs burrowing in the silt of the same reach. It is winter and there are no adults flying. The individual has been absent for all but a day of this interval.

Half a year on, nothing of the individual remains in any form. Its eggs hatched in the autumn and the nymphs are now overwintering in the riverbed. The adult itself was gone within forty-eight hours of the first description.

After six months the question concerns the river, not the insect. The mayfly's atoms are distributed through fish, birds and sediment, and its descendants are young nymphs in the mud. There has been no mayfly for a hundred and eighty days.
1year: A year later a new generation of the same species is emerging on the same riffle, but the original animal has been gone for three hundred and sixty-four days. Its offspring are approaching their own emergence. Nothing of the individual is identifiable.

One year on, the evening swarm above the river looks exactly as it did and contains none of the same insects. The described mayfly ended in a single night; the pattern it belonged to has completed one full turn without it.

After a year the cycle has closed without the individual. The species is present, the riffle is the same gravel, the swarm rises at the same hour. The mayfly described has been dead for all but a fraction of the interval.
10years: Ten years later the mayfly is ten generations gone. The population has persisted through droughts and a pollution incident that thinned it badly in one summer. Nothing traceable to the individual survives except an unmeasurable share of ancestry.

After a decade the river still supports the species at reduced density; the riffle has shifted a few metres and the willow has fallen in. The described animal is one of many millions of such insects since, all of them dead.

A decade has passed for a creature whose whole adult existence was a day. The lineage continues; the individual has been absent for all but a ten-thousandth of the interval and has left no recoverable trace whatever.
100years: A century later the species is still on the river, its abundance halved by nutrient enrichment and warming. A hundred generations separate the present swarm from the described animal. The individual is unrecoverable in every sense.

After a hundred years the mayfly's lineage may or may not include any part of it; drift and selection have long since dissolved any particular contribution. The reach has been dredged once and has recovered. Adults still emerge in June.

A hundred years have produced a hundred generations. The river runs warmer, the hatch is earlier by a fortnight, and the willow bank has been replaced by rip-rap. The insect described lasted one evening of that century.
1000years: A thousand years later the species may still be present, but its populations have been broken and reassembled by a millennium of climate and land use. A thousand generations lie between. The individual is a statistical zero.

After a millennium the river itself has changed course within its floodplain and the described riffle no longer exists. Mayflies of some species emerge from the new gravels. Nothing connects them to the described animal but deep ancestry.

Ten centuries is a thousand generations for this insect. Whatever lives on the river now is measurably different in genetics and in timing. The mayfly of the first description ended within a day and left only diffuse inheritance.
10000years: Ten thousand years later the river has been reorganised by a changing climate and the insect fauna with it. Ten thousand generations have passed. Descendants may exist as a diverged population or not at all; the individual is meaningless at this scale.

After a hundred centuries the lineage has either speciated, migrated or been extirpated locally at least once. The gravel the eggs were laid on is somewhere downstream and buried. Nothing of the animal, its cohort or its habitat persists.

Ten millennia is long enough for the species to have shifted its range across a continent. The described mayfly is ten thousand generations of drift away from anything now flying, and has been dead for all but one day of that.
1000000years: A million years later the genus persists but the species almost certainly does not. A million generations is ample for speciation and extinction several times over. The river, the riffle and the animal are all gone without residue.

After a million years mayflies still emerge somewhere, as they have for three hundred million years, but no line of descent can be traced to this one. The individual's day of adult life is an unmeasurable instant in the interval.

A million years dissolves even the species. The described insect belonged to a population on a river that no longer exists, in a climate that has since flipped many times. Only the order Ephemeroptera is continuous.

t0: The asteroid is an irregular S-type body about 1.2 kilometres across, orbiting in the main belt with a period of four years. Its surface is bare regolith and rubble, heavily cratered, and it rotates once every eleven hours.

At first the object is a dark, potato-shaped rock of roughly 1.2 kilometres, a loosely bound rubble pile under a thin regolith. It orbits between Mars and Jupiter and turns on its axis every eleven hours.

A 1.2-kilometre main-belt asteroid of silicate and metal, cratered on every scale down to centimetres. It has no atmosphere, no internal activity and a four-year orbit; its surface temperature swings by a hundred kelvin each rotation.
1day: One day later the asteroid is unchanged except in position: it has moved about 1.5 million kilometres along its orbit and turned on its axis just over twice. No feature of its surface has altered in any detectable way.

A day on, the rock is identical. It has advanced a fraction of a degree along its path and completed two rotations. Micrometeorites have struck it, adding nothing measurable to a surface already saturated with craters.

After twenty-four hours nothing about the body has changed but where it is. Its shape, mass, rotation rate and surface are the same to any precision we can state. It is a million and a half kilometres further along.
1week: A week later the asteroid has travelled some ten million kilometres and rotated fifteen times. It is otherwise exactly as described: the same shape, the same craters, the same rubble. Space weathering over seven days is immeasurable.

Seven days on, only the orbital phase has moved. The body has passed through roughly one two-hundredth of its year. Its surface, its spin and its mass are unaltered by anything that has happened. Seven days is nothing to a body with no processes to run.

After a week the asteroid is in a different place and no other respect. Solar wind has darkened its surface by an amount no instrument could resolve; the craters, ridges and boulders are where they were.
6months: Six months later the asteroid has covered an eighth of its orbit, some four hundred million kilometres, and rotated four hundred times. Physically it is unchanged: the same 1.2 kilometres, the same rubble-pile structure, the same cratered face.

Half a year on, the only difference is position and the illumination and temperature that follow from it. There has been no geological activity of any kind. The object is the same object, further round its ellipse.

After six months the asteroid has moved forty-five degrees along its path. Nothing has hit it larger than a grain. Its shape, spin period and surface remain as described, to the limits of measurement. Half an orbital season has passed and the rock has not responded.
1year: One year later the asteroid has completed a quarter of its orbit and is unchanged in every other respect. It has rotated about eight hundred times. No crater on it is new at any size a telescope could see.

A year on, the body has moved a quarter of the way round its orbit and is otherwise identical. Unlike anything on a planet it has no seasons, no weather and no erosion; only its position has advanced.
After a year the asteroid is exactly the rock it was, in a different part of the same ellipse. Its mass is the same to within a few tonnes of accreted dust and a few tonnes of ejected material.
10years: Ten years later the asteroid has gone round two and a half times and is physically the same. Its spin has been altered by sunlight by a fraction of a second in the period, and a metre-scale crater may be new. Nothing else has changed.

After a decade the object is unchanged except in position and, immeasurably, in spin. The YORP effect has been at work on it for ten years, which at this size amounts to nothing. The surface looks identical.

A decade has moved the asteroid two and a half orbits and left it otherwise untouched. No impact large enough to reshape it has occurred, and the regolith has been stirred by micrometeorites to a depth of microns.
100years: A century later the asteroid has completed twenty-four orbits and remains the same body. Its rotation period has drifted by a second or so under radiation torques, and its surface has been darkened very slightly by the solar wind.

After a hundred years the rock is unchanged at any scale that matters. Position and orbital phase are the only large differences; a few small craters have been added and about the same number erased by seismic shaking.

A century of main-belt existence has done nothing visible. The asteroid is 1.2 kilometres across, cratered and inert, on the same orbit with slightly precessed elements. It has gone round the Sun twenty-four times. The body's shape and mass are as they were in every respect.
1000years: A thousand years later the asteroid has made two hundred and forty orbits and is still the same object. Its orbit has precessed measurably and its spin has been changed by a few percent. The body itself is unaltered.

After a millennium the asteroid remains physically as described, with a slightly different spin state and a thoroughly shifted orbital position. A few ten-metre-scale impacts may have occurred somewhere on it; the shape is the same.

Ten centuries in the belt has left the rock intact. It has been struck by countless grains and nothing large. Its orbit has drifted within the resonance structure of the belt, and its surface is as it was.
10000years: Ten thousand years later the asteroid has orbited two and a half thousand times. Its spin may have been substantially altered by radiation torques, and one crater of a few tens of metres is likely new. It is still the same 1.2-kilometre body.

After a hundred centuries the object is recognisably identical. Its orbital elements have wandered, its rotation has spun up or down, and a handful of small impacts have redistributed regolith. Nothing has broken it apart.

Ten millennia has produced no change that would alter the description. The asteroid is wherever its orbit has taken it, cratered as before, with perhaps one fresh bright scar and a slightly different rotation axis.
